chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hassan, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurara, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about the skilled woman, upon whom it is stipulated at the time of the marriage contract that he will come to her whenever he wishes, every month, and every Friday for a day, and from the expenses such and such. He (peace be upon him) said: 'That stipulation is not valid (of itself). And whoever marries a woman, she is entitled to what is due to women regarding maintenance and sharing of time. However, if a woman marries and fears ill-conduct from him, or fears that he will marry another woman in addition to her, or that he will divorce her, and she reconciles with him regarding her rights for something from her maintenance or her share of time, then that is permissible, there is no problem with it.'

key_terms.النُّشُوزِ: Ill-conduct, neglect, or estrangement by the husband
key_terms.الْقِسْمَةِ: Sharing of time (between co-wives or regarding conjugal rights)
key_terms.الْمَهَارِيَّةِ: The skilled/competent woman (often referring to a wife with specific qualities or status)
key_terms.فَصَالَحَتْهُ: She reconciled/settled with him (via a compromise agreement)

ai.seo_question: What are the valid stipulations a wife can make in a Shia marriage contract regarding intimacy and maintenance?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies that while the husband's general right to intimacy is inherent, specific contractual stipulations regarding frequency or fixed maintenance are not automatically binding unless part of a mutual compromise (sulh). This ruling highlights the Shia legal principle of flexibility in marriage contracts, allowing wives to voluntarily waive rights like maintenance or conjugal time to secure protection against neglect, polygamy, or divorce, thereby emphasizing the consensual nature of marital obligations.
